beats.narration_text: Can you trust a number an AI hands you? A number can look completely normal and still be wrong, and the usual checks won't catch it. Only one thing does.

props.command: Can you trust a number an AI hands you?
props.topic: HUMANITARIANS AI · MYCROFT — SEC FILINGS AGENT
output: A number can look perfectly normal and still be wrong.
Only a source you didn't derive it from will.

beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Asavari, a fellow at Humanitarians AI. This video is about how to trust a number an AI hands you. In a couple of minutes you'll learn a simple check that catches wrong numbers even when they look completely normal, using a real bug from a tool I built on SEC financial data. If you work with data or AI outputs and want to avoid confident mistakes, this is for you.

props.command: What is this video about, and why should I watch it?
props.topic: HUMANITARIANS AI · MYCROFT — SEC FILINGS AGENT
output: Who: Asavari, a Humanitarians AI fellow
Why watch: catch the mistake before it costs you

beats.narration_text: This is a real revenue figure my tool first produced for Microsoft. Correctly formatted, right range, passes every structural check. It's also wrong, by two years. Nothing flagged it, because nothing had anything to compare it against.

props.artifactTitle: A plausible number is the dangerous kind
artifactLines: Correctly formatted · in the right range

beats.narration_text: The tool trusts nothing by default and checks in two ways. Deterministic rules catch impossible values, a margin over a hundred percent, a balance sheet that doesn't balance. But a plausible wrong number sails through those. To catch it, you compare against a figure you did not derive from the same data. And every number keeps a link back to its filing.

props.artifactTitle: Two kinds of wrong, two kinds of check
artifactLines: Deterministic rules catch the impossible (margin > 100%, unbalanced sheet)
A ground-truth cross-check catches the plausible (vs a figure you didn't derive)
Provenance: every value links back to its filing

beats.narration_text: Here's the moment it mattered. Group the data by the filing's own year field and you get two hundred eleven point nine billion, and it looks fine. Cross-check it against Microsoft's actually reported revenue, two hundred eighty-one point seven billion, and the mismatch is obvious. The self-consistent version passed. Only the independent check caught it. And the correct figure carries its exact tag and filing link, so it's verifiable.

props.artifactHeading: Self-consistent PASS vs independent CAUGHT IT
artifactLines: Trust the filing's fy field -> FY2025 = $211.9B -> PASS (looks fine)
Cross-check vs reported -> Microsoft FY2025 = $281.7B -> MISMATCH -> CAUGHT IT
props.sparkLine: Only the independent check caught it.

beats.narration_text: The honest limit. A number can be correctly tagged, well formed, and still wrong. No stack of rules fixes that, because the rules share the data's blind spot. The cross-check is the one test that doesn't, because it comes from outside the data.

props.artifactTitle: No rule replaces a known-good reference
artifactLines: Correctly tagged + well-formed + wrong period -> passes rules, fails the cross-check
The rules share the data's blind spot
The cross-check doesn't — it comes from outside

beats.narration_text: So next time an AI hands you a number, run four checks. Can you trace it to its source? Is there a rule that catches the impossible? Can it say I don't know? And the one that matters most, did you check it against something you didn't derive from the same data? Fail that last one, and you're just trusting a number because it looks clean.

props.artifactTitle: Trust the check you didn't derive from the data
props.artifactHeading: Run this on any number an AI hands you
artifactLines: Can you trace it to its source?
Is there a rule that catches the impossible?
Did you cross-check it against a source you didn't derive from?

beats.narration_text: Same Number, Two Ways. From Humanitarians AI.
